analysis.one_liner: Strips the tax deduction for most big-bank executive bonuses unless pay is half stock and vests over five years.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have denied big banks a tax break on executive bonuses. Under current law, companies can deduct performance-based pay without limit; this bill would have let big financial firms deduct such pay only if at least half of it came as company stock, it vested over at least five years, executives could not hedge or insure away their own pay risk, and CEOs and CFOs forfeited bonuses if the company restated its books because of misconduct. It would have covered banks with more than $25 billion in assets, and required annual public reports on their pay practices. It never got a hearing.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, ordinary taxpayers would gain: banks above roughly $25 billion in assets would no longer be able to write off unlimited executive bonuses against their taxes, and the extra tax revenue would otherwise be borne by everyone else. Rank-and-file bank employees would also gain some assurance that the pay of the 25 highest earners — and anyone whose bets materially affect the firm's risk — is tied to long-term results rather than short-term deals.

how_it_helps.text: It removes the tax deduction for most incentive pay at big banks unless that pay is at least half stock, vests over at least five years, and cannot be hedged or insured by the executive — aligning pay with long-term results rather than short-term bets.
It ends the deduction for pure commission-style pay at these firms, curbing volume-driven bonus structures like those in mortgage sales.
It requires CEOs and CFOs to forfeit incentive pay if the company must restate its books because of misconduct, and requires annual public reports on each bank's pay practices.

analysis.who_pays: Top executives and highly paid risk-takers at large banks, whose deferred bonuses over $1 million would become nondeductible to the employer unless they met the long-vesting, stock-based requirements. Their compensation would not be capped, but a larger share would be tied up in company stock for five years or more.

drawbacks.text: Tying pay to employer stock can push executives to focus on short-term share prices, which critics of stock-based pay argue contributed to the risk-taking behind the financial crisis.

The rules would apply only to banks and financial firms above roughly $25 billion in assets, so large non-financial companies and smaller firms would face no equivalent limits, and talent could shift to them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main drawback is the risk that pushing top banker pay into long-vesting stock encourages short-term stock-price moves rather than sound risk-taking, and that high performers at large banks could relocate to smaller ones. Against that, the bill aimed only to deny a tax break for outsized pay, not to cap pay, and it targeted the sector whose pay structures helped drive the financial crisis. It died without a hearing or a vote, so none of these tradeoffs were ever tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Nelson introduced the bill on March 22, 2010; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks and financial firms keep deducting unlimited incentive pay from their taxes; nothing in the bill ever became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large banks keeping unlimited bonus deductions

for.name: Sen. Bill Nelson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee; no other senator cosponsored it.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Sen. Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: As the chairman of the committee of referral, held the authority to schedule a hearing or markup; none was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a vote, so no roll-call positions were recorded; it had zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Large banks and financial firms (over $25B in assets)
industries.note: The bill would deny a tax deduction for most incentive pay at these firms unless it met strict long-term vesting and stock requirements, directly cutting the after-tax value of executive bonuses.
The bill requires external compensation reviews and certifications, creating new work for consultants who audit pay practices.
The bill directs the Treasury Secretary to write extensive new rules on hedging, valuation, and anti-abuse tests, expanding compliance work for advisers to large financial firms.
